definition: Ability to recognize previously encountered distinctive odors.

The ability to manipulate the spotlight of attention flexibly to focus on task-relevant stimuli and ignore task-irrelevant stimuli. Sometimes referred to as spotlight or focal attention, focus, control of attention, executive controlled attention, or executive attention.
The speed at which written words can be copied.
Knowledge or sensitivity to nonverbal human communication/interaction systems (e.g., facial expressions and gestures).
The ability to rapidly draw or sketch as many things (or elaborations) as possible when presented with a nonmeaningful visual stimulus (e.g., a set of unique visual elements).
Ability to precisely and skillfully coordinate arm-hand positioning in space.
Knowledge about the function, terminology, and operation of ordinary tools, machines, and equipment.
The ability to rapidly think of different ways of expressing an idea.
The ability to form a link between two previously unrelated stimuli such that the subsequent presentation of one of the stimuli serves to activate the recall of the other stimuli.

The ability to rapidly produce words that share a phonological (e.g., fluency of retrieval of words via a phonological cue) or semantic feature (e.g., fluency of retrieval of words via a meaning-based representation).
The ability to understand speech. Starts with comprehending single words and increases to long complex verbal statements.

The ability to quickly and accurately survey (visually explore) a wide or complicated spatial field or pattern with multiple obstacles and identify a target configuration or identify a path through the field to a target end point.
An intermediate stratum ability reflecting the general understanding of spoken language at the level of words, idioms, and sentences. The ability to comprehend and communicate using language.
Ability to make quick specific or discrete motor movements of the arms or legs.
The ability to rapidly call objects by their names.
Knowledge of finger-spelling and signing (e.g., American Sign Language).
Consistency in the rate of alternating between different visual perceptions.
The ability to remember narratives and other forms of semantically related information.
The ability to rapidly produce a series of ideas, words, or phrases related to a specific condition or object. Quantity, not quality, is emphasized.
Time required to silently read a passage or series of sentences as quickly as possible.
Reaction time to one of two or more alternative stimuli, depending on which alternative is signaled.

The ability to distinctly hear phonemes, blend sounds into words, and segment words into parts, sounds, or phonemes. Also referred to as phonological processing, phonological awareness, and phonemic awareness.
Range of scientific knowledge (e.g., biology, physics, engineering, mechanics, electronics).
Reaction time where the stimuli must be compared for a particular attribute.
Ability to exert precise control over muscle movements, typically in response to environmental feedback (e.g., changes in speed or position of object being manipulated).
The ability to retain (on a short-term basis) auditory codes such as tones, tonal patterns, or speech sounds.
Range of general knowledge about mathematics.
The ability to reason logically using known premises and principles.
Ability to quickly combine disconnected, vague, or partially obscured visual stimuli or patterns into a meaningful whole, without knowing in advance what the pattern is.
The speed and fluency of generating or copying words or sentences. Also listed under Grw and Gps.
The ability to encode and maintain verbal information in primary memory.
The speed of arm and leg movement.
The speed, fluency, and accuracy in manipulating numbers, comparing number patterns, or completing basic arithmetic.
The ability to rapidly think of a number of solutions to a particular practical problem.
The ability to voluntarily mentally produce very vivid images of objects, people, or events that are not actually present.
Reaction time to the presentation of a single visual or auditory stimulus.
The ability to perceive complex visual patterns and mentally simulate how they might look when transformed (e.g., rotated, changed in size, partially obscured, and so forth).
The speed and fluency of looking up and comparing visual stimuli that are side-by-side or more widely separated in an extended visual field.
The ability to detect and discriminate differences in speech sounds (other than phonemes) under conditions of little or no distraction or distortion.
The ability to recognize and maintain a musical beat.
The speed and fluency of searching or scanning an extended visual field to locate one or more simple visual patterns.
Knowledge of writing in the English language with respect to capitalization, punctuation, usage, and spelling.
The breadth and depth of knowledge that one's culture deems essential, practical, and worthwhile for everyone to know.
Ability to recall as many unrelated items as possible, in any order, after a large collection of items is presented.
Ability to discriminate and judge tonal patterns in music with respect to melodic, harmonic, and expressive aspects (phrasing, tempo, harmonic complexity, intensity variations).
The ability to copy or generate text quickly.
Ability to resist being affected by this capacity involving geometric figures.
Ability to maintain the body in an upright position in space or regain balance after balance has been disturbed.
Ability to comprehend connected discourse during reading.
The ability to hear words or extended speech passages correctly under conditions of distortion or background noise.
Ability to make precisely coordinated movements of the fingers (with or without the manipulation of objects).
Competence in the ability to understand communication from others by watching the movements of their mouths and expressions.
Ability to speak in real-life situations (e.g., lecture, group participation) in an adult-like manner.
Ability to precisely and fluently execute a sequence of eye-hand coordination movements for positioning purposes.
Ability to perfectly identify the pitch of tones.
Range of geographic knowledge.
The ability to solve problems quickly by using mental rotation of simple images.
The ability to encode and maintain visual information in primary memory.
Ability to write with clarity of thought, organization, and good sentence structure. (Not clearly defined by existing research.)
Ability to apprehend and identify a pictorial or visual pattern when parts of the pattern are presented rapidly in serial or successive order.
Ability to find, apprehend, and identify a visual figure or pattern embedded in a complex visual array, when knowing in advance what the pattern is.
Knowledge or awareness of the grammatical features of the native language.
Ability to rapidly perform successive articulations with the speech musculature.
The ability to rapidly produce a series of original or useful ideas related to a particular concept.
Ability to make precisely coordinated movements of a hand or a hand and the attached arm.
Ability to rapidly produce original, clever, and insightful responses (expressions, interpretations) to a given topic, situation, or task.
Ability to exert muscular force to move (push, lift, pull) a relatively heavy or immobile object.
Similar to Language Development (LD) but for a foreign language.
The ability to reason with quantities, mathematical relations, and operators.
The knowledge of the definitions of words and the concepts that underlie them. Vocabulary knowledge.
The ability to observe a phenomenon and discover the underlying principles or rules that determine its behavior.
The speed at which differences in stimuli can be perceived.
The ability to remember complex visual images over short periods of time (less than 30 seconds).

An intermediate stratum ability reflecting the speed and fluency with which similarities or differences in visual stimuli (e.g., letters, numbers, patterns) can be searched and compared in an extended visual field.
Measured mathematics achievement.
The speed and fluency of reading text with full comprehension. Also listed under Grw.
Reaction time when the decision requires some encoding and mental manipulation of stimulus content.
The ability to rapidly draw different solutions to figural problems.
More specific or narrow oral communication skills than reflected by Communication Ability (CM).

The time taken to physically move a body part (e.g., a finger) to make the required response. May also measure the speed of finger, limb, or multilimb movements or vocal articulation (diadochokinesis).
Ability to localize heard sounds in space.
Ability to spell. (Not clearly defined by existing research.)
Ability to recognize and decode words or pseudowords in reading.
Ability to accurately estimate or compare visual lengths and distances without using measurement instruments.
